articleTitle: Illumination and some of its fundamental considerations
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: To some, the subject with which this paper treats may, at first thought, appear to be simple, and compared with other branches of engineering, relatively insignificant. When, however, we stop to consider and analyse the important part that artificial lighting plays in almost every sphere of endeavour, it becomes apparent that it is a subject of the utmost importance. Our home comforts, pleasures, industrial activities, safety along the streets after dark, and in travel, are all influenced to the greatest degree by artificial illumination.

articleTitle: The first electric steel melting furnace in South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The President: You see on the table here some carbons, and as the subject of carbons is naturally very closely associated with electric furnaces, it might be as well if we were to make it known that four out of the five have been locally made. (Applause). Through the medium of Mr. Webb, those carbons, which have been made on the Nourse Mines, are here for your examination to-night. It might be stated briefly that carbon making for furnaces is one of those very secret processes, and the manufacture of the carbons very often spells success or failure to the furnace. No doubt many of you are acquainted with the fact that early attempts in the Transvaal have been met with great difficulty. It is easy to describe the question of carbon making; it is easy to describe the purification, the grinding and the treatment, both of the carbon itself and the adhesive mixture, whether it be pitch, treacle, or anything else, also the moulding and the baking, and the subjecting to the proper pressure. The various points in the process, however, require a great deal of skill. Mr. Webb was good enough to invite me to see these carbons working in a furnace with a current of nearly 300 amperes. He also gave me the privilege of seeing some of the calcium carbide manufactured.

articleTitle: Small generating stations and electricity supply schemes
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate): It is with great pleasure and interest I have followed the discussion at your meetings on the subject of small generating and electricity supply schemes in South Africa by Mr Botting and other members. I welcome a discussion on the above subject as it tends to bring forward information that may be of some assistance to the isolated engineer who seldom comes in contact with the other members of his profession. I must agree with Mr. Castle in his statement: That small electrical stations, as a rule, are a patched-up box of freaks — erected without any consideration for local conditions or future development. The instruments are the cheapest procurable, repairs have to be done in many instances under the worst conditions regarding tools and skilled labour, his assistant (or learner as he is called) is usually a budding Edison of 20 or 24 years of age, who starts at a salary of &£5 per month (less if possible) and a promise that if he works hard and the scheme pays he may get more. He no doubt does his best, but it is with great difficulty that anything like a good job can be done or a correct log book can be kept in the engine room.

articleTitle: Overwinding and controlling devices for winding-engines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Member): Mr. Newbery's paper brings to our notice one of the most important points in connection with electric hoisting on these fields: I might say of all hoisting, “The Safety First Aspect.” It is hoped that this paper will be thoroughly discussed by our members, and as the author and Mr. Dew have said, it would be instructive if descriptions of the various devices in use which are intended to minimise the risk of accident were brought forward for discussion. In the first place, it appears to me, from the author's description and diagram, that he has eliminated the “Call Bell” system in the shaft where his apparatus was installed. If this is so, I fail to see how the system can comply with Regulation 29 under the Mines and Works Act. If such is not the case and a “Call Bell” also is used, the running of an additional wire right through the shaft is necessary, and the cost of this in a deep level mine would probably be prohibitive. It is not essential, nor is it, I think, usual, under local hoisting conditions, for the engine-driver to reply to the skipman's signals for the hoisting of rock. He receives the 1 bell signal for raise and immediately starts hoisting; but, when hoisting men, the driver first receives 3 bells, to which he must reply. Bearing this point in mind, I would like to describe to members an arrangement suggested by my father some years ago, by which the overwinding prevention device or limit switch in the headgear for men could be controlled. The ordinary 3-wire bell system would be used, but before the driver could reply to any signals for hoisting men, he would have to put in a plug in the battery wire to his pull. This plug would carry an arm, which, when in the “on” position, opens the contacts “C” controlling the men limit switch, and thus permits it to operate and trip the main switch should an overwind occur. The plug is withdrawn when rock hoisting is to take place, closing the contacts and thus permitting the rock limit switch only to come into operation. The connections for this arrangement are shown by the dotted lines in the figure.

abstract: (Member): I am pleased to have an opportunity to contribute some remarks towards the discussion on this most interesting paper. The subject is specially interesting at the present time, in view of the projected S.A.R. electrification, and I express my warm appreciation of the missionary and educational work Mr. Kirk-land has been engaged on since July, 1917. I would like to record not only my appreciation of the paper itself, which is full of interesting data and suggestion, but also my admiration for what must constitute one of the General Electric Co.'s greatest achievements in the railway electrification line. With this understood, I shall now proceed to offer such criticisms as occur to me, and shall venture to put before the members of this Institute other data concerning railway electrification, which, while perhaps not strictly arising out of the subject matter of the paper under discussion, does arise in connection with some of the inferences the author has ventured to draw.

abstract: (Member): Mr. du Pasquier's paper brings before us a subject which has been and still is a bone of contention between the manufacturer and the purchaser, the manufacturers as a body naturally endeavouring to produce and sell machines with a minimum of redundant material, while the aim of the purchaser is to secure as much for his money as possible. In discussing the subject of the maximum permissible temperature it is as well to consider why it needs any discussion at all, and consideration makes it clear that there are involved two limits or extremes, e.g., limit (a), the case where the current and flux are run so high that the machine burns out in delivering its rated output; and limit (b), the case where the provision of iron and copper is so liberal that the machine does not have any appreciable rise in temperature when on full load.

articleTitle: Exhibition of mining apparatus, etc.

abstract: The Presidant: The members of our Institute will be aware of the fact that the Council had under consideration some time ago the question of arranging a local exhibition of mining apparatus and other macninery, which has been manufactured locally, due to circumstances arising out of the war. In this respect, it is my pleasure to inform you that a letter has been received from the South African Institution of Engineers, asking this Institute to join in the combined efforts of the kindred societies, such as the South African Institution of Engineers, the Chemical Metallurgical and Mining Society, and so on. Your Council will be asked at its next meeting to appoint three members, and I am sure it will be a great pleasure to join in the combined effort to show the results of local efforts in the development of local industries and local manufactures.

articleTitle: Relay protective devices
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate Member): I notice that this interesting and valuable paper of Mr. Monk's is marked down in the agenda as “final for discussion” to-night, and whilst there is not much that one can discuss in the paper, it has occurred to me that a short description of a simple method of obtaining approximate short circuit currents might be of interest to members. This question really arises indirectly out of the paper, since in applying any protective scheme it is necessary to determine the short-circuit currents which will be available under all conditions. It is, perhaps, unfortunate that the term “overload” has ever come into use in connection with sectionalising distribution systems, because it implies that the relays should be set to operate at a value determined by the normal load on the feeder. Such a setting is possible if definite-time-relays are used, but where a relay having inverse-time characteristics is used, it is necessary to consider the current that occurs during times of trouble, and that may be tens or even hundreds of times greater than the normal current. An approximate method of determining the possible short-circuit current is by observing the voltage drop between two stations at normal load.
